title: What Are Microservices Really All About_ (And When Not To Use It)

segments.text: Microsoft Services Architecture enables large-teamed to build scalable applications that
are composed of many loosely coupled services. What is a typical microservices architecture
look like and when should we use it? Let's take a look. Microsoft services are loosely coupled.
Each service handles a dedicated function inside a large-scale application. For example,
shopping card, billing, user profile, push notifications can all be individual microservices
these functional areas are sometimes called domains. Microsoft services communicate with each other
via well-defined interfaces with small service areas. There's small service areas,
limit the blast radius of failures and defects. It makes each service easier to reason about
in the context of the entire application. Microsoft services talk to one another over a combination
of remote procedure calls or RPC, events streaming or message brokers. RPC, like GRPC,
provides faster response but the blast radius or the impact other microservices will be larger
when the service was to go down. Events streaming provides better isolation between services
but they take longer to process. Microsoft services can be independently deployed since each
service is smaller, easier to reason about and has a smaller blast radius. This gives the
operators peace of mind and confidence to deploy often. Microsoft services provide more flexibility
to scale up individual microservices independently. The operational flexibility is invaluable.
Well architected microservices practice strong information hiding. This often means
breaking up a monolithic database into its logical components and keeping each logical
component well hidden inside is corresponding microservice. By logical component it can
mean a separate schema within a database cluster or an entirely separate physical database.
This is an implementation detail. However, one big drawback of microservices is to
breaking up of the database. By breaking up a database into separate logical units the database
can no longer maintain foreign key relationships and enforce referential integrity between these
units. The burden of maintaining data integrity is now moved into the application layer.
Now let's take a look at other critical components required for a successful implementation
of microservices architecture. A key component is an API gateway. API gateway handles incoming
requests and routes them to the relevant microservices. The API gateway relies on an identity
provider service to handle the authentication and authorization of each request coming through
the API gateway. To locate a service to route an incoming request to the API gateway consults a
service registry and discovery service. Microservices register with this service registry
and discover the location of other microservices through the discovery service.
There are other useful components in a microservices architecture,
like monitoring and alerting, depth ops tool links for deployment and troubleshooting for
example. Let's wrap up by discussing when to use microservices architecture.
Microservices costs money to build and operate. It will only only make sense for large teams.
For large teams, it enables team independence. Each domain or function can be independently
maintained by a dedicated team in a well-designed microservices architecture. These independent
teams can move fast and the plus radius of failures is well contained. Each service could be
independently designed, deployed and scaled. However, the overhead of a sound implementation is
so large that it is usually not a good fit for small startups. One device for startups
is to design each function in the application with a well-defined interface. One day,
if the business and team are growing fast, that microservices architecture starts to make sense,
it will be manageable to migrate. You would like to learn more about system design,
check out our books and weekly newsletter. Please subscribe, you'll learn something new.
Thank you so much and we'll see you next time.
